newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: Separatist re-elected in Moldova's Dnestr region. [CORRECTED 12:47 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Separatist re-elected in Moldova's Dnestr region. [CORRECTED 12:47 GMT]

text.p: Igor Smirnov, leader of Moldova's rebel Dnestr region since 1991, was re-elected for another five years in a local election held on Sunday, the head of the regional electoral commission said.

Pyotr Denisenko said on Monday that Smirnov took 71.94 percent of the vote. His rival, Vladimir Malakhov, polled 19.83 percent. Turnout was 57.3 percent (corrects from 71.94 percent) of the 428,000 electorate, Denisenko told Reuters from the regional capital Tiraspol.

Neither Smirnov, a 55-year-old Soviet-era industrial boss, nor his rival offered any softening of the mainly Russian and Ukrainian-speaking region's secessionist stance toward the rest of Moldova, where the majority speak a language identical to Romanian, spoken across the border.

Both Malakhov and Smirnov, who was first elected on December 1, 1991, called for the continued presence of 6,000 Russian troops, who have policed a ceasefire since a civil war in 1992 between Dnestr rebels and Moldovan forces that killed hundreds.
Smirnov told reporters in Tiraspol on Sunday that the elections were held "to show the world that Dnestr is a democratic state set up in line with international standards".
"Our state exists de facto," he said. "These elections are another step towards the legal recognition of our state."
But no country recognises Dnestr independence.

Russia, Ukraine and the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) have been pressing for a compromise and the new Moldovan president, elected three weeks ago, has pledged to grant Dnestr autonomy in return for peace.
Dnestr broke away from the rest of Moldova in 1991 on fears its people could lose out if Chisinau moved closer to Romania.
But the region's Soviet-era industry, typified by the sort of plant Smirnov used to run, has stagnated economically.
Though still one of Europe's poorest nations, the mainly agricultural Moldova has implemented free market reforms that have begun to bear some fruit.
East of the Dnestr river, however, bread is rationed and crime and violence common, leaving many in the region nostalgic for the stability of Soviet days and hoping for Russia's help.

Moldovan president-elect Petru Lucinschi, who takes office on January 15, has pledged to use his good contacts in Moscow to press Dnestr leaders into a compromise, but remains adamant against secession.
"These elections will have no political or legal effect," Lucinschi said last week.

Smirnov, who says "ties with Russia are a priority for the mostly Slav region", wants his unrecognised republic to be an equal participant of the Commonwealth of Independent States -- a loose grouping of 12 former Soviet republics.
But Russia, the dominant force of the CIS, fought a bloody war against its own secessionists in Chechnya and would not smile upon such an outright disintegration close to its borders.
